Framewise

Paper in preparation

One recording in, finished demo out.

Upload a raw screen recording. Framewise watches it, decides what to cut and where to zoom, writes the narration, casts a voice and renders a finished demo video in 11 languages.

View code on GitHub
~$0.03per video
42edit decisions
64events in 229s
11languages

The problem

Shipping a product demo takes a chain of people. Someone writes the script, an editor cuts the dead air and adds zooms, someone records the voiceover, and a localization vendor repeats it all for every language. That's days of work, per video, per language.

Features in action

Each word highlights as it's spoken.

Eases in on the exact UI element in use.

MusicGen bed that ducks under the voice.

Translation

ElevenLabs for English, Sarvam for 10 Indic languages.

ElevenLabs · Misa · English narrator

Edit plan · 229s → 86s
6 cuts19 zooms4 speed ramps

Smart edits

42 decisions: cuts, zooms, speed ramps and clicks.

What it does

  • Understands the recording. Builds a timestamped log of every click, scroll and UI change.
  • Edits, not just narrates. Cuts dead air, speed-ramps repetitive stretches and adds animated zooms aimed at the exact UI element in use.
  • Writes and voices the narration in 11 languages, with an LLM casting the speaker from about 11,000 voices.
  • Speaks like a real tech creator. Technical terms stay in English inside Tamil or Hindi narration.
  • Finishes the video. Word-level captions, click ripples, a branded backdrop and locally generated background music.

How it works

Eight agents orchestrated with LangGraph, sharing one state. Here is how they connect:

Screen recording
Agent 1Frame Extractor
Agent 2 · bypassedCursor Detector
Agent 4Audio
Parallel join
Agent 3 · GeminiVision
Agent 8Theme & Voice
Agent 5Analysis
Agent 6Script Planner
Agent 7 · localMusicGen
FFmpegDual render
Two final videos

Agent 2 is bypassed: cursor detection is folded into the vision agent, which reads the video in 60-second windows.

  1. Frame Extractor samples frames with FFmpeg.
  2. Cursor Detector is folded into vision analysis.
  3. Vision uses Gemini to watch the video in 60s windows and log every action.
  4. Audio transcribes existing narration and detects silence.
  5. Analysis merges vision and audio into one timeline tagged cut, zoom or keep.
  6. Script Planner writes the narration and the concrete edit plan.
  7. Music generates an intro sting and a looping bed with MusicGen.
  8. Theme and Voice picks a backdrop from the app's colours and casts the voice.

The render engine then applies cuts, speed ramps, zooms, click effects, narration, music and captions, and renders twice, once per voice engine (ElevenLabs and Sarvam), so you pick the better take.

Why 60-second windows?

A single Gemini request over a long video only described its first minute. It returns a fixed budget of about 20 to 25 events regardless of length, and still reports success. Overlapping 60s windows give each stretch its own budget: 64 events across 229 seconds, with the largest gap at 15s.

Languages

English, Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Bengali, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi and Odia. Indian languages use Sarvam's native TTS rather than a Western model approximating them.

AI

Gemini, ElevenLabs, Sarvam Bulbul v3, MusicGen

What's next

The script planner sometimes under-writes long videos, leaving a quiet tail, and Sarvam renders don't yet get word-level captions. Both are on the list, alongside the research paper.

IndicF5 Code-Switch TTS

Open source

Because nobody says कार्यालय when they mean office.

Text-to-speech for Indian languages that pronounces the English words people actually mix in. A fine-tune of AI4Bharat's IndicF5 on real Hindi-English speech.

Model on Hugging Face Code Demo

मैं आज office जा रहा हूँ, morning में एक important meeting है और उसके बाद team के साथ new project discuss करना है।

6 / 6English words recovered
71%lower English CER
0loss on pure Hindi
8unseen languages improved

The problem

Indians don't speak pure Hindi or pure English. We say office, meeting and project in the middle of Hindi sentences. IndicF5 reads those English words with Indic phonetics and turns them into gibberish: office came out as अफे, important meeting as टहौर का निये.

Voice cloning

Record about 10 seconds of your voice, and the model speaks any Hinglish sentence in that voice. Here it is cloning mine.

Also ships with 10 built-in voices: Hinglish, Tamil-Hinglish, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi and Telugu.

How I fixed it

Adapter-style QLoRA training on a frozen 0.3B IndicF5 backbone, using real Hindi-English speech from OpenSLR-104, sized to fit a single Kaggle session.

It works beyond Hindi

Trained on Hindi-English only, yet English pronunciation improves in 8 languages it never saw. Same sentence: "I'm going to office today, there's an important meeting in the morning."

And nothing was forgotten: pure Tamil output is character-for-character identical to the base model, and Telugu and Bengali differ by a single character.

Try it

from transformers import AutoModel
import soundfile as sf

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "Tharshan/indicf5_hindi-english_code_switch", trust_remote_code=True)

ref, ref_text = model.voice("ritu_hinglish")
audio, sr = model.generate(
    "मैं आज office जा रहा हूँ, morning में एक important meeting है।",
    ref_audio=ref, ref_text=ref_text)
sf.write("out.wav", audio, sr)

Self-contained: weights, vocabulary and 10 reference voices ship in the repo. Clone any voice from a short clip and its transcript.

What's next

Pure English is better than base but still drops words on long input, generation handles one or two sentences at a time, and timbre is slightly duller because the training audio came from an ASR corpus. Next up is Tamil-English, trained on natural code-switched speech.

Research Agent

From a topic or a DOI to a podcast you can listen to.

Why

Finding, reading and summarising research papers by hand takes hours, and there's nothing to listen to on the go. I wanted research to be accessible to students and researchers short on time.

What

A multi-agent system that fetches papers, summarises them, groups them by topic, writes a synthesis and narrates it as podcast-style audio with citations. It accepts a topic, a DOI or a PDF.

How

Five agents run in sequence, each handing its output to the next:

  • Fetcher agent. Searches CrossRef by topic or resolves a DOI, then downloads open-access PDFs through Unpaywall.
  • Extractor agent. Pulls clean text from each PDF with pdfplumber and PyMuPDF, and summarises it with Llama 3.3 70B.
  • Classifier agent. Embeds each paper with Sentence Transformers and assigns it a topic using the LLM.
  • Topic synthesizer agent. Merges all summaries within a topic into one readable synthesis.
  • Media and citation agent. Formats a citation list and converts each synthesis into an MP3 podcast.

Results

  • Automated the full research workflow, cutting manual effort by about 70%.
  • Concise, accurate syntheses across multiple papers.
  • Ready-to-play MP3 podcasts, plus structured JSON and citations.

Tech

Llama 3.3 70B · Sentence Transformers · pdfplumber · gTTS · FastAPI · Streamlit

BankEase AI

A fine-tuned banking chatbot.

Why

General-purpose LLMs give vague, generic answers to everyday banking questions. Customers need clear, specific replies, however they phrase the question.

What

A banking chatbot built by fine-tuning Llama 2-7B chat on banking queries, so it answers in a focused, structured way. The model and dataset are published on Hugging Face.

How

  • Data. A banking dataset of about 1 million queries and answers, with many phrasings of the same question.
  • Model. Llama 2-7B chat loaded in 4-bit NF4 with double quantisation, so a 7B model trains on Google Colab.
  • Fine-tuning. QLoRA adapters (rank 64, alpha 16, dropout 0.1) trained with TRL's SFTTrainer, paged AdamW and a 2e-4 learning rate.
  • Release. Merged and pushed the fine-tuned model and the dataset to the Hugging Face Hub.

Results

  • A 7B banking assistant fine-tuned on a single Colab GPU with 4-bit QLoRA.
  • Consistent answers across different phrasings of the same question.
  • Open model and dataset on Hugging Face for anyone to reuse.

Tech

Llama 2 · QLoRA · PEFT · bitsandbytes · TRL · Hugging Face
